clinicalPearls: RCC accounts for 90-95% of malignant neoplasms arising from the kidney; the remaining 5-10% are transitional (urothelial) cell carcinomas of the renal pelvis (covered separately in Chap. 91) (p.687-688).

The classic triad of hematuria, flank pain, and a palpable abdominal mass is now uncommon; most tumors are detected incidentally on cross-sectional imaging (CT/MRI) performed for other reasons (p.688-689).
Other presenting features include fever, weight loss, anemia, and a varicocele (p.688).
Once called the "internist's tumor" because it was frequently first detected via a paraneoplastic syndrome before modern imaging was common (p.688-689).
Clear cell is the predominant histology (~70% of cases) and is found in >80% of patients who develop metastases; it arises from epithelial cells of the proximal tubules (p.688).
Any solid renal mass should be considered malignant until proven otherwise; a definitive diagnosis is required (p.689).
Most common sites of distant metastasis are the lungs, lymph nodes, liver, bone, and brain; the clinical course can be unpredictable and protracted (p.689).
RCC is associated with anecdotal reports of spontaneous regression (p.687).
Increasing detection of incidental low-stage tumors has improved 5-year survival and increased use of nephron-sparing surgery (partial nephrectomy) (p.689).
harrison.pathophysiology: RCC is a heterogeneous group of tumors. Most cases are sporadic, but familial forms exist. Clear cell RCC (the predominant subtype) is characterized by loss of chromosome 3p as the earliest event, causing loss of heterozygosity for 3p genes including VHL, PBRM1, BAP1, and SETD2. VHL encodes a tumor-suppressor protein that regulates transcription of VEGF and other effectors via ubiquitination of hypoxia-inducible factors (HIF); VHL inactivation upregulates VEGF signaling, promoting tumor angiogenesis and growth and rendering clear cell RCC susceptible to antiangiogenic therapy. Clear cell RCC also arises in von Hippel-Lindau syndrome (autosomal dominant, VHL gene on chromosome 3p), which carries a ~70% lifetime risk of clear cell RCC. Papillary subtypes are linked to activating MET mutations or gain of chromosome 7; chromophobe tumors originate from the distal nephron and typically show aneuploidy. Early loss of chromosome 9p confers high risk of early metastatic dissemination and correlates with poor cancer-specific survival (p.687-688).
additionalDifferentials: Inflammatory lesions: pyelonephritis or renal abscess (p.689)
Transitional (urothelial) cell carcinoma of the renal pelvis (p.689)
Metastases from cancers originating in other organs (p.689)
infectionMimics: Pyelonephritis (inflammatory renal lesion in the differential of a renal mass) (p.689)
Renal abscess (inflammatory renal lesion in the differential of a renal mass) (p.689)
additionalInvestigations: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis - part of standard evaluation of a suspected renal tumor (p.689)
Chest radiograph; CT of the chest if metastatic disease is suspected on chest x-ray (p.689)
MRI - useful for evaluating inferior vena cava when tumor thrombus/invasion is suspected, or when IV contrast for CT is precluded by impaired renal function (p.689)
Needle biopsy to confirm histology in small tumors managed with radiographic surveillance before delayed surgery (p.689)
redFlags: Constitutional symptoms: fever, weight loss, anemia (p.688)
Paraneoplastic features: erythrocytosis, hypercalcemia, nonmetastatic hepatic dysfunction (Stauffer's syndrome) (p.688)
harrison.prognosis: Staging uses the AJCC TNM system. Stage I tumors are <=7 cm and confined to the kidney; stage II are >7 cm and confined to the kidney; stage III extend through the renal capsule but remain within Gerota's fascia, grossly infiltrate the renal vein, or involve regional nodes (N1); stage IV invades adjacent organs or involves nonregional nodes or distant metastases. About 65% present at stage I-II, 15-20% at stage III, and 15-20% at stage IV. Overall 5-year survival is currently ~77% but varies greatly by stage. For metastatic disease, the IMDC risk model uses six factors associated with worse survival (poor performance status, low hemoglobin, high serum calcium, high neutrophils, high platelets, and <1-year interval from diagnosis to systemic treatment). Zero risk factors confer significantly longer median survival (>=5 years) than one to two factors (~4 years) or three to six factors (~3 years) with first-line checkpoint-inhibitor-containing regimens. Projected overall survival for newly diagnosed metastatic disease has tripled over the past 15-20 years (p.688-690).
pitfalls: Relying on the classic triad (hematuria, flank pain, palpable mass) for diagnosis - it is now uncommon, and most tumors present incidentally (p.688-689).
Assuming chemotherapy will help - metastatic RCC is refractory to cytotoxic chemotherapy; treatment relies on molecularly targeted agents and checkpoint immunotherapy (p.689).
Treating a solid renal mass as benign without proof - any solid renal mass should be considered malignant until proven otherwise (p.689).
Despite many candidate biomarkers investigated for predictive value in metastatic RCC, none have been validated for clinical use to date (p.690).
Renal vein or inferior vena cava invasion does not preclude surgical resection if no metastases are present (p.689).
harrison.severityClassification: AJCC TNM staging (stages I-IV; Fig. 90-1): Stage I <=7 cm confined to kidney; Stage II >7 cm confined to kidney; Stage III extends through renal capsule within Gerota's fascia, infiltrates renal vein, or N1 nodal involvement; Stage IV invades adjacent organs or has nonregional nodal or distant metastases. For metastatic disease, the IMDC (International Metastatic RCC Database Consortium) risk model stratifies prognosis using six clinical/laboratory factors (p.688-689).
management: Partial (nephron-sparing) nephrectomy for localised tumours where feasible, with radical nephrectomy reserved for larger or more advanced disease
Offer active surveillance or thermal ablation for small renal masses, particularly in older or comorbid patients, using needle biopsy to confirm histology when surgery may be delayed

Treat metastatic clear cell disease with systemic therapy exploiting VHL-driven angiogenesis, combining immune checkpoint inhibitors with VEGF tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as axitinib, cabozantinib or lenvatinib
Consider cytoreductive nephrectomy and metastasectomy in selected patients with metastatic disease
Provide supportive and palliative care for advanced disease, including bone-directed therapy and radiotherapy for symptomatic metastases and management of paraneoplastic syndromes and anaemia
Undertake structured post-treatment surveillance with cross-sectional imaging and renal function monitoring to detect recurrence and protect the remaining kidney
Refer for genetic counselling and screening when hereditary disease such as von Hippel-Lindau syndrome is suspected, and manage complex cases through a uro-oncology multidisciplinary team
